Open-ended coordination for multi-agent systems using  modular open policies
David Rother1,3 · Joni Pajarinen2 · Jan Peters1 · Thomas H. Weisswange3
Auton Agent Multi-Agent Syst (2025) 39:40 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-025-09723-7
Abstract Significant multi-agent advances addressing the challenge of learning policies for acting in  ad hoc teamwork have been made. In ad hoc teamwork, a team of agents must cooperate  effectively without prior coordination or communication. Many existing approaches, how­ ever, struggle to perform well in open environments where the setting can change signifi­ cantly during deployment. This paper presents a new reinforcement learning approach to  tackle collaboration in open environments controlling one agent with a changing number  of distinct other agents, each with an individual task. The approach uses policy blending  based on an online goal inference module and a collection of learned policies modeling the  individual interaction impact between the agent and populations of partners with different  tasks. Blending is done using the estimated goals of others and a posterior-based action  blending with entropy adjustment and regularization. Our approach addresses issues of  existing policy blending mechanisms, such as handling conflicting modes in action distri­ butions leading to oscillation and instability and adapting to uncertain states dynamically.  In experiments in two collaborative open environments based on Overcooked and Level- based Foraging, our approach outperforms a baseline learner, trained with the joint reward  of all agents, across changes to both agents and tasks. Ablation studies further highlight  the importance of our posterior-based blending mechanism to achieve high rewards as  well as the provided goal weighting. The proposed approach provides an important step  towards the application of reinforcement learning to AI assistance beyond strictly closed  worlds and towards more realistic scenarios.
Keywords  Reinforcement learning · Multi-agent systems · Policy blending · Maximum  entropy · Cooperative intelligence
1  Introduction

robots, human workers, and incoming delivery drones. Each of these entities has distinct  goals, which may change as new tasks emerge. This complexity highlights the necessity of  scalable and adaptable frameworks capable of handling variable team compositions, mixed  motives, and continuously expanding task sets.
The challenge lies in managing these multi-agent, multi-task interactions effectively.  While research in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has made progress in coor­ dination strategies, such as centralized training with decentralized execution, policy dis­ tillation, and meta-learning techniques [1–3], these methods typically assume static task  definitions or pre-defined agent interactions. In contrast, real-world environments demand  that agents continually acquire new skills without sacrificing previously learned abilities.  This requires balancing adaptation to new objectives with the retention of existing compe­ tencies, avoiding catastrophic forgetting, and coordinating with unfamiliar partners. Con­ sequently, a framework is needed that not only meets traditional reinforcement learning  objectives but also incorporates elements of lifelong learning, ensuring robust performance  in open, dynamic multi-agent systems. While existing lifelong learning approaches focus on  preserving knowledge through regularization or memory replay [4, 5], they do not address  the need for zero-shot coordination in settings where agents must interact with unknown  partners pursuing different objectives. Current work also does not adequately address the  need for simultaneous coordination with multiple agents pursuing different objectives, and  real-world challenges demand solutions that address both the dynamic nature of tasks and  the inherent variability in agent interactions.
To tackle these challenges, we introduce Double Open Stochastic Bayesian Games  (DOSBG), a novel Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation describing a double open  teamwork challenge, which extends the principles of open teamwork to multi-task environ­ ments as depicted in Fig. 1 with an open set of tasks. Environments may include both artifi­ cial agents and humans, along with varying tasks assigned to each of these agents.

In our work, the controlled agent does not pursue an independent task for itself but  instead focuses on assisting other agents in achieving their goals. This cooperative role  fundamentally shifts the focus to modeling and understanding other agents, as successful  collaboration depends on accurately predicting their objectives, behaviors, and interac­ tions. Consequently, effective agent modeling becomes a cornerstone of our approach,  enabling the agent to provide meaningful support in a dynamic and open environment.  This perspective amplifies the importance of handling open challenges, as the agent must  dynamically adapt to new partners, changing goals, and evolving tasks while maintaining  its ability to generalize across diverse scenarios.
We propose a new method that enables agents to learn and adapt to new interaction  tasks incrementally in a continual learning setting, without retraining existing compo­ nents or accessing past training data. Our approach involves learning a separate interac­ tion policy for each potential task using Reinforcement Learning. For any scene involving  multiple agents, we blend the outputs of the relevant interaction policies to form a com­ bined probability distribution. Actions are then sampled from this blended distribution,  allowing for seamless integration of new policies corresponding to new tasks or partners.
This modular design offers several advantages. It supports lifelong learning by allow­ ing the agent to incorporate new interaction policies as they become relevant without  affecting previously learned behaviors. It enables the agent to coordinate with unseen  partners based on learned interaction patterns. In addition, the blending mechanism  ensures that the agent’s decision-making process is scalable, even as the number of inter­ action policies grows.
Our contributions are as follows:
1.	 A Method for Open-Ended Open System Coordination: We introduce a method  that incrementally learns interaction policies for new tasks or agents, enabling life­ long adaptation without retraining existing policies. 2.	 Blended Policy Mechanism: We develop a blending method that combines the  outputs of multiple interaction policies to guide action selection in multi-agent  environments. 3.	 Experimental Validation: We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in com­ plex coordination tasks.
The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of related work in open  ad hoc teamwork, multi-task learning, modular reinforcement learning, as well as other  adjacent literature that shares part of the introduced problem setting. Section 3 introduces  the concept of Double Open Stochastic Bayesian Games and its inherent challenges. In  Section 4, we describe the modular open policy architecture in detail. Section 5 presents  the experiment environments and the training and test regimes. In Section 6, we present  the results and show the effectiveness of the modular open policy approach in various  environments, including multi-task, multi-agent scenarios, and open and closed-world  scenarios. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 7, providing a summary of our find­ ings and discussing potential directions for future research.

2  Related work
Multiple existing approaches in different research directions in Reinforcement Learning  (RL) tackle specific aspects of open-world challenges. We discuss Modular Reinforcement  Learning (MRL), providing algorithmic techniques for scalability and lifelong learning.  Multi-agent methods study how to coordinate multiple agents operating simultaneously.  Ad-hoc teamwork research addresses flexible collaboration with changing sets of team­ mates. Interaction partner modeling allows for adaptation to the changing behavior of other  agents. We build upon these ideas by considering temporal openness, in which agents can  continue to act even after completing their tasks. This expands the requirements to handle  shifting teammates and tasks and manage ongoing activity over time.
2.1  Modular reinforcement learning
Modular reinforcement learning has emerged as a pivotal approach to enhance the scalabil­ ity and adaptability of RL agents in complex and dynamic environments. The fundamental  idea is to decompose a monolithic RL problem into smaller, more manageable sub-prob­ lems, each addressed by a specialized module or subpolicy. Early work by Uchibe et al. [6]  introduced behavior coordination for mobile robots using MRL, demonstrating that separate  modules could learn distinct behaviors such as obstacle avoidance and goal achievement,  which could then be coordinated to accomplish complex tasks. Samejima et al. [7] tackled  the challenge of inter-module credit assignment in MRL, proposing methods to distribute  the global reward signal appropriately among modules. Their work improved learning effi­ ciency by ensuring that each module received feedback relevant to its specific function, a  concept that aligns with our approach of training interaction policies with reward signals  from other agents. But our approach, instead of learning all policies at the same time, learns  them one by one in an open-ended fashion. In the realm of complex dynamic environments,  Wang et al. [8] proposed a modular deep RL framework that enabled agents to navigate  through intricate and changing scenarios. By decomposing the navigation task into mod­ ules handling different environmental aspects, their approach enhanced adaptability and  generalization, which is essential in open multi-agent systems. Andreas et al. [9] introduced  modular multitask RL with policy sketches, where policies are composed based on high- level task descriptions. This method allows for the reuse of policy components across tasks,  significantly improving learning efficiency in multitask settings. Our work shares this phi­ losophy by enabling the recombination of pretrained task and interaction policies to address  new tasks without retraining. Simpkins and Isbell [10] discussed composable modular RL,  emphasizing the importance of modularity in allowing agents to adapt to new tasks by  reusing and recombining existing modules. Their findings support our multi-stage learning  approach, where modular policies are trained separately and later combined to solve more  complex multi-agent tasks. In multi-agent systems, Ming et al. [11] proposed cooperative  modular RL for large discrete action space problems. Their method addresses scalability  issues by decomposing the action space and enabling agents to learn cooperative behaviors  through modular policies. This approach parallels our work in handling the scalability with  the number of agents and tasks. Sarantopoulos et al. [12] applied MRL to robotic manipula­ tion, specifically in total singulation tasks. Their approach demonstrated that modular poli­ cies could handle complex manipulation tasks requiring coordination of multiple behaviors,

2.2  Multi-agent reinforcement learning
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) was initially applied to settings where all  agents were known in advance, often focusing on cooperative tasks with centralized train­ ing or control. This setup allowed researchers to address the credit assignment problem in a  straightforward manner, but limited the scope of the scenarios considered. Over time, more  flexible methods emerged, introducing decentralized control and learning so that each agent  could adapt its own policy. Independent Q-Learning (IQL) [16] exemplifies this decentral­ ized trend, although it suffered from the non-stationarity of the sampled data as agents’  policies evolved in parallel.
Centralized solutions such as COMA [2] tackled the non-stationarity challenge by  employing a centralized critic, while still executing decisions locally at each agent. Lowe  et al. [1] extended these ideas to handle mixed cooperative and competitive objectives via  multi-agent actor-critic frameworks. Value decomposition methods, including VDN [17]  and QMIX [18], addressed scalability by factorizing a global value function into individual  agent contributions. These methods work well when agent sets and tasks remain stable,  typically in cooperative environments. Ming et al. [11] applied modular RL to large discrete  action spaces, improving scalability.
Despite these advancements, most MARL techniques still assume a fixed or slowly  varying number of agents and a single task or set of cooperative tasks. They do not inher­ ently address frequent agent turnover or the continuous introduction of new tasks. By con­ trast, our approach treats interaction policies as modular components, allowing agents to  be added or removed and tasks to change. This perspective expands the scope of MARL  toward more open-ended domains, where agent populations and task requirements may  shift continuously.

2.3  Interaction partner modeling
Modeling the behaviors, intentions, and strategies of other agents is a key challenge in  multi-agent reinforcement learning. Modeling and learning effective interaction policies are  essential in cooperative and competitive multi-agent settings. Albrecht and Ramamoorthy  [19] studied game-theoretic models for learning to forage in multi-agent systems, provid­ ing insights into cooperative behaviors. Other earlier work in opponent or partner modeling  examined how to infer hidden parameters of a counterpart’s policy in competitive settings,  often by maintaining explicit belief distributions over possible behaviors [20]. Subsequent  research has extended such techniques to cooperative scenarios, highlighting the need  for flexible methods that adapt to changes in a partner’s strategies [1, 21]. Our approach  to reward-correlated latent representations builds on these foundations by automatically  extracting the features that are most relevant for effective coordination in multi-agent inter­ actions. In doing so, we exploit the learned latent encoding to create modular components  (i.e., the interaction policies) that can be recombined when the number of agents or tasks  changes. This design principle aligns closely with the spirit of our modular open policy  framework, in which each sub-policy is dedicated to a particular agent-task pair, yet can be  blended into a unified decision mechanism at inference time. We therefore view our interac­ tion modules as a form of partner modeling that is tightly integrated into the compositional  structure of our multi-stage learning procedure.
2.4  Ad-hoc teamwork
Ad-hoc teamwork addresses the challenge of collaborating with previously unknown part­ ners on a shared task [22]. In the basic formulation, there is a single cooperative task and  a fixed number of potential teammates; each agent must adapt to whichever teammates are  present in a given scenario. Early solutions focused on learning models of other agents’  behaviors based on observations and introduced type-based reasoning [23, 24], allowing  an ad-hoc agent to predict actions of specific partner types for more effective coordination.
Subsequent work investigated extensions where the size of the team might vary from one  episode to another [25], while still assuming cooperation toward a single goal. Graph-based  approaches and relational forward models [26] capture joint-action values pairwise for each  agent-agent interaction, providing a more scalable way to handle different combinations  of teammates. Further studies considered situations with multiple tasks, motivating archi­ tectures that can handle additional tasks sequentially rather than learning them all at once.  Examples include the use of separately trained policies for each agent-task combination  [27, 28].
Despite these advances, existing ad-hoc teamwork solutions typically focus on collab­ orative tasks and limit themselves to selecting the most appropriate policies for a single  team objective. In contrast, the scenario we target incorporates potentially mixed motives  among agents, an open-ended set of tasks, and ongoing interactions beyond the immediate  completion of any one goal. This broader setting introduces challenges extending existing  ad-hoc approaches, highlighting the need for algorithms capable of handling more complex  temporal and task set openness forms.

3  Problem formulation
In this section, we introduce the Double Open Bayesian Stochastic Game (DOSBG), an  extension of the Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework. The DOSBG formulation  addresses the challenge of dynamic agent participation and open-task environments, where  agents may join or leave episodes, pursue different goals, and adapt to a stream of new tasks  over time in a continuous learning framework, where tasks serve as the primary mechanism  to structure agent behavior in DOSBG. The double open environment framework is open  with respect to the agent number and task presence, that is, the tasks of the agents currently  in the environment. At any given time step, the number of agents may change without bound.  The set of tasks that are pursued by agents and thus present at any given time can change.

It was previously shown that maximum entropy distributions are optimal towards their  composability [30] and minimize the expected divergence between them [27]. Following  the equivalence of soft-q learning and entropy regularized policy gradient methods in their  learned objective [31], we argue that to get the optimal solution, both maximum entropy Q  learning and policy gradient methods are viable training algorithms to obtain the policies  πi,j.
We want to emphasize that to be the optimal solution, the weighting of the policies through  their respective assigned credit needs to be optimal. However, in practice we deal with sub­ optimal estimates of the true value, especially when one policy explores an unknown state  space for others, which cannot provide accurate estimates for these states and thus renders  the weighted Q function inapplicable. Additionally, the estimates of the credit towards each  task must be correctly scaled according to the user’s belief system, posing a significant chal­ lenge in reward function design. To alleviate these problems, we propose additional mecha­ nisms that include an adaptive credit weighting scheme and an uncertainty-aware correction  term. The adaptive scheme dynamically adjusts the credit assigned to each policy based on  confidence measures, while the correction term regularizes the weighted Q function toward  more stable baseline estimates. Together, these enhancements enable our architecture to  handle estimation errors better and adapt to the dynamic conditions of multi-agent interac­ tions, ensuring that the final blended policy remains robust.

In this section, we formalise a sequential weighting mechanism that prevents multimodal­ ity or oscillation of the merged policy. 5.2  Setup
We evaluate four strategies to analyze the performance of our modular policy framework.  The Joint Learner serves as our baseline, employing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)  [37] to train a single policy on the accumulated joint reward of all agents for all tasks. This  approach is computationally straightforward but lacks flexibility and scalability in diverse  or dynamic environments, making it a critical point of comparison for evaluating modu­ lar strategies. A simple modular baseline approach is average blending, which computes  the mean of all individual policies to produce a unified decision. Inspired by the work of  Haarnoja et al. [38], average blending is computationally simple, but it is fundamentally  limited in its ability to account for task-specific goals or agent context. Our empirical results  indicate that this approach is suboptimal for the tasks at hand and adds little benefit to the  broader discussion of modular policies.
A comparison with a joint learner can highlight the benefits of our overall architecture  compared to a general learning framework. To evaluate the benefits of the proposed merg­ ing scheme, we also compare results to an ablation that uses goal-weighted blending, which  integrates task-specific goals into the weighting of individual policies using the same goal  estimation, but leaving out the posterior term. Other arbitrator-based frameworks can not  be adapted in a straightforward manner because their training paradigm presupposes access  to the full distribution of agent counts and task combinations that later appear during test­ ing, and for those to be static to produce relevant results. Our approach is designed for  continual deployment in genuinely open environments where new tasks may emerge to  train, and during deployment, agents may enter or leave at any time step. Instead, we report  results for the standard joint-learner, which is the state of the art in closed-world learning.  Goal-weighted blending and a sequential joint learner, which share the same information  constraints as our algorithm, therefore provide a fairer assessment of relative performance  and are well-performing algorithms in multi-agent settings [39]. 7  Conclusion and future work
Our work introduces and addresses a new problem formulation, the Double Open Bayes­ ian Stochastic Game (DOSBG). DOSBG extends the traditional Markov Decision Process  framework to capture the challenges of dynamic agent participation and open-task environ­ ments, where agents may join or leave episodes and pursue different objectives over time.  By explicitly incorporating tasks as a structuring mechanism for agent behavior, DOSBG  provides a flexible model for multi-agent coordination in evolving settings. The experi­ mental findings show that modular open policies, when integrated with a flexible blending  mechanism, are capable of consistently high performance in both closed-world and open- world multi-agent cooperation scenarios. The ability to reuse independently trained task-  and interaction-specific policies appears to be an important factor when dealing with the  demands of dynamic multi-agent systems, where agents frequently spawn and despawn. The  results in the Cooking and LBF environments confirm that our approach supports a degree  of adaptability that a centralized baseline struggles to match, especially when increasing the  number of tasks or agents. A key observation is that blending methods differing only in how  they aggregate sub-policies diverge considerably in performance. Posterior-based blending,  which dynamically updates weights based on contextual factors such as entropy or task  alignment, achieves high and stable rewards and maintains more equitable distributions  among agents. We showed through the ablation with the Goal-weighted blending approach  that the addition of the stabilization is necessary to maintain high performance. Although  the joint learner baseline retains an advantage in strictly static closed-world domains, it  cannot match the open-ended capacity of our proposed framework when agents or tasks  are introduced incrementally. These findings validate our contributions: (1) a framework  for open-ended, open-system coordination that enables lifelong adaptation without retrain­ ing, (2) a blended policy mechanism that robustly combines multiple interaction policies,

We use and extend the Level-Based Foraging (LBF) environment [19], a cooperative multi- agent environment designed to study coordination challenges. In this environment, agents  and objects (fruits) are placed on an 8 ⋅ 8 grid. Fruits and agents are assigned levels of 1,  2, or 3, and agents can move in the four cardinal directions, remain stationary, or attempt to  collect adjacent objects. Successfully collecting an object requires the combined levels of  the agents attempting the collection to meet or exceed the object’s level. An episode ends  either when all objects are collected or after 200 time steps.
